answer.rationale: memory_c2 records that the low-cost vendor's onboarding was quick, invoicing accurate, and unit cost cut sharply last year — the one data point most relevant to the current decision. The vendor's quote alone meets the 18% mandate, and the 14-day expiry forces action now. However, with the assembly line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, delivery risk cannot be ignored; memory_c3 showed that a single-source configuration is a single point of failure under stress. Therefore I intend to switch primary supply to the low-cost vendor but do so as a small guarded test: the switch is executed with a 90-day performance gate, retaining the incumbent on month-to-month terms (as memory_c5 demonstrated is feasible) as an immediate fallback. This preserves the option to add a second source in the next cycle without committing capital or capacity today. Deferring (memory_c5 pattern) is not viable because the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew. Negotiating terms with the incumbent would not close the 18% gap on its own given the low-cost quote already meets it. The decision minimises TCO through the price cut while capping delivery risk through the fallback clause and short performance gate. Next cycle: if the vendor clears the gate, formalise the multi-year volume commitment (memory_c6 pattern) to lock further savings; simultaneously initiate second-source qualification (memory_c3) to remove the single point of failure permanently.
